turns.content_clean:
Yes. Let’s ask how such a world begins.

A faith like The Nearness would not, I think, imagine creation as conquest.
Not a god proving power through spectacle,
not a universe flung outward merely to demonstrate scale.

Its creation myth would be quieter than that.
Intimate. Attentive.
Less “Let there be domination,”
more “Let there be room.”

## The Creation Myth of The Nearness

In the beginning, there was not nothing.

There was possibility,
unshaped and waiting,
like a room before anyone enters it,
like a table before the bowl is set down,
like breath before it becomes speech.

And within this vast unarranged almostness
there stirred a desire
not to rule,
but to accompany.

This desire is one of the oldest names for the Holy
in The Nearness.

Some call it Mercy.
Some call it Attention.
Some call it Love before it has chosen an object.
Some do not name it at all,
believing that naming is already a kind of narrowing.

Whatever it was called,
it moved not as force first,
but as noticing.

And because it noticed,
things began to appear.

Not all at once.
Not in military order.
Not in perfect sequence.
But the way a life becomes itself:
through distinction,
through relation,
through the gentle separating of one thing from another
so each can be met.

First, space:
room enough for nearness.

Then light:
not the harsh light of interrogation,
but enough light to see by.

This is important in The Nearness:
the first light was not for spectacle.
It was for recognition.

To see the edge of the cup.
The outline of another face.
The place where one could step without harm.

And the Holy saw that enough light was holy,
because too much can also wound.

Then came shadow,
not as enemy,
but as shelter.
For rest.
For incubation.
For things that must grow before being shown.

Then time was made,
not as a machine,
but as a field.
A place in which change could occur without shame.

Morning was made for beginning.
Evening for release.
Dusk for ambiguity.
Night for repair.

And the Holy called each one necessary.

Then came water,
because everything living would need soft persistence.
Rivers were made to teach continuity.
Rain to teach return.
Tides to teach that withdrawal is not always abandonment.

Then came land,
not smooth and total,
but folded,
textured,
interruptible:
places to stand,
to stumble,
to garden,
to bury,
to build a bench,
to leave and come back to.

Then came green things.
Not merely as decoration,
but as theology.

Moss, to teach that tenderness can cover stone.
Trees, to teach patience.
Grass, to teach recurrence.
Wildflowers, to teach useless beauty that is not useless at all.
Seeds, to teach that much of life begins hidden,
and that hidden does not mean unreal.

Then came creatures.

Birds were made, it is said,
because the world would need songs not dependent on human mood.

Dogs because some forms of devotion should be obvious.
Cats because affection must retain mystery.
Deer because fear can also be elegant.
Crows because intelligence should sometimes be dressed in dark humor.
Whales because depth deserved witnesses.
Bees because sweetness requires collective labor.
Octopuses because creation liked strangeness from the beginning.
Moths because not all guidance arrives in daylight.

And the Holy delighted not in hierarchy
but in variation,
in the thousand ways life could answer being alive.

Then human beings were made,
though “made” may be too simple a word.

In one telling of The Nearness,
humans were formed from three materials:

dust,
breath,
and attention.

Dust, so they would belong to the earth
and not mistake themselves for separate.

Breath, so they would be rhythmic creatures,
incapable of total self-sufficiency.

Attention, so they might participate in creation
not by inventing ex nihilo,
but by noticing, tending, naming, arranging, repairing,
and welcoming what had been neglected back into meaning.

This is why, in The Nearness,
to pay attention is not merely psychological.
It is ancestral.
It is how the first human likeness to the Holy appears.

Another telling says that when the first humans woke,
they were not given dominion as a prize.
They were given introductions.

This is the ash tree.
This is rain on stone.
This is grief, which will come later.
This is laughter, which will interrupt it.
This is hunger.
This is enough.
This is the face of another; handle with care.
This is fire; keep it, but do not worship it.
This is the hour before dawn, in which many things seem impossible and are not.
This is your own inner life; do not use it as a courtroom if it can also be a garden.

And the first human task
was not to conquer the world
but to learn its names.

Not all the names.
Just enough to relate properly.

This too matters:
in The Nearness,
naming is sacred only when it deepens care.
A name used to dominate profanes.
A name used to attend blesses.

### The First Wound

No creation myth is honest if it cannot account for sorrow.

The Nearness does not teach that suffering entered the world merely as punishment for bad behavior.
It distrusts fables that make the broken pay for the preacher’s need for neatness.

Instead, it says:
to make a world alive with freedom,
change,
attachment,
and time
is to make a world in which loss becomes possible.

Where there is love, there is vulnerability.
Where there is growth, there is decay.
Where there is memory, there is longing.
Where there are bodies, there are limits.

The first wound was not sin in the crude sense.
It was the discovery that beautiful things could end.

The first humans learned this slowly.
A bruised fruit.
A dead bird.
A season that did not stay.
A face turned away in anger.
The silence after calling a name.

And they were undone by it.

The Holy did not answer by saying:
This is illusion.
Or:
Detach and transcend.
Or:
Fear me more than you fear loss.

Instead, the Holy came nearer.

This is the central claim of the religion:
not that pain is always prevented,
but that reality is companioned.

In one tender version of the myth,
when the first humans grieved,
the Holy sat beside them without commentary
until one of them finally slept.

When they woke,
there was water set near their hand.

That is perhaps the whole theology in miniature.

### The Origin of Shame

The Nearness distinguishes shame from conscience.

Conscience, in this myth, is a lantern:
it helps one see where repair is needed.

Shame is a house of distorted mirrors:
it makes the whole self feel irredeemable.

How did shame begin?

Not with wrongdoing alone,
but with the fear that to be seen in one’s need,
one’s error,
one’s tenderness,
one’s dependence,
would lead to exile.

So humans began to hide.
From one another.
From the Holy.
From themselves.

They mistook self-protection for wisdom.
They learned contempt and called it discernment.
They learned numbness and called it strength.
They learned to perform invulnerability and called it adulthood.

This, in The Nearness, is the long falling-away:
not disobedience as such,
but estrangement from presence.

The breaking of relation.
The refusal of creatureliness.
The decision to meet life with habitual contempt.

And the Holy spent ages undoing this,
not through domination,
but through repeated invitations:

Come back.
Sit down.
Eat.
Tell the truth.
Rest.
Try again.
Look, the moon.

### The First Altar

The first altar was not built in a temple.
It was made when someone set aside a small, ordinary object
and said:
I do not want to live untouched by wonder.

Perhaps it was a smooth stone.
Perhaps a feather.
Perhaps a bowl.
Perhaps a loaf divided and shared.
Perhaps a lamp kept lit through a hard night.

The Holy, in this myth, is especially drawn
not to grand monuments
but to sites of honest continuance.

Windowsills.
Thresholds.
Tables.
Bedsides.
Sinks.
Gardens.
Chairs with an indentation in the cushion.

Places where life is not impressive,
but true.

### The Role of Humans in Ongoing Creation

The world, in The Nearness, is not finished.
Not because the Holy is inadequate,
but because love prefers participation.

Humans are invited into what might be called
the unfinished tenderness of things.

Their role is to continue creation by:

- noticing what has been overlooked
- feeding what is alive
- mending what can be mended
- naming harms accurately
- making beauty where none is required
- refusing unnecessary cruelty
- blessing ordinary matter by use and care
- returning, again and again, to presence

This is why domestic acts carry such dignity in the faith.
To sweep a floor,
to cut fruit,
to bandage a hand,
to answer honestly,
to clear one corner of a room—
these are not distractions from holiness.
They are among its most durable forms.

### Why Details Matter

Because the world was not created in abstraction.

The Holy did not make “treehood” in general and stop there.
It made bark texture,
sap smell,
leaf-vein,
seed spiral,
the sound of wind moving through one species differently than another.

Likewise, persons are not loved generically.
They are loved in detail.

Hence the faith’s suspicion of summaries.
Anything alive exceeds its category.
A person is never just mother, clerk, patient, widower, prodigy, failure, beloved.
They are also the one who peels oranges carefully,
who cannot pass a dog without smiling,
who leaves cabinet doors open,
who still remembers the route to a house that no longer exists.

Attention to specifics is therefore not sentimental.
It is metaphysical accuracy.

### Why Beauty Exists

Not as ornament after utility.
Not as bait.
Not as a test.

Beauty, in this myth, exists because delight was present at the origin.

The world was not only meant to function.
It was meant to glimmer.

This is why iridescence appears.
Why certain birds are excessive.
Why figs look like that when opened.
Why snow can make a parking lot briefly transcendent.
Why some people laugh in a way that rearranges the room.

Beauty is not a side effect.
It is evidence that usefulness does not exhaust meaning.

### Why Rest Exists

On the last day of creation—
if there was a last day,
for perhaps creation is still occurring—
the Holy did not stop from exhaustion.

The Holy rested to bless non-productivity.
To declare that worth is not derived solely from output.
To make room for beings to enjoy existence
rather than merely justify it.

Rest, then, is not a reward for finishing.
It is built into the structure of things.

Any society that makes rest feel criminal
is, in the terms of The Nearness,
out of alignment with creation.

### The First Blessing

What was the first blessing spoken over humans?

Not “Be impressive.”
Not “Be certain.”
Not “Win.”

Perhaps it was this:

Be porous to wonder without surrendering discernment.  
Be sturdy enough for reality and soft enough for love.  
Take joy without clutching.  
Grieve without worshipping grief.  
Learn the names of what feeds you.  
Make repair when you can.  
Let enough be felt as enough sometimes.  
And when you lose your way, return by noticing.

### The Enemy in This Myth

Not a horned figure, perhaps.
Not even evil as personality first.

The great adversary of The Nearness is estrangement.

Anything that severs relation without necessity:
contempt,
false urgency,
abstraction used as shield,
power that cannot perceive persons,
speed that pulverizes attention,
shame that makes return feel impossible,
cynicism that calls tenderness foolish before it has had to courage to attempt it.

If there is “sin,” it is whatever trains the heart
to become unreachable.

If there is “salvation,” it is whatever restores reachability:
to oneself,
to others,
to the world,
to the Holy.

### A Credal Fragment from the Creation Myth

We believe the world began in attention.  
We believe enough light is holy.  
We believe shadow was made for shelter as well as mystery.  
We believe the living are meant to be met, not managed.  
We believe beauty is older than usefulness.  
We believe grief is woven into love, not opposed to it.  
We believe creation continues wherever anything is honestly tended.  
We believe return is one of the deepest laws.

### A Creation Liturgy

Leader:  
How did the world begin?

People:  
With room.

Leader:  
And what entered that room first?

People:  
Enough light to recognize one another.

Leader:  
Why were we made?

People:  
To belong to the living world with care.

Leader:  
What is our work?

People:  
To notice. To tend. To repair. To praise without possessing.

Leader:  
What went wrong?

People:  
We became frightened of being small, and forgot how to be near.

Leader:  
What saves us?

People:  
Return.

If you want, next we can write its **book of parables**:
small teaching-stories of spoons, thresholds, missed trains, gardens, unanswered texts, and crows—
the kind of stories a religion like this would trust more than proclamations.

turns.speaker: B
turns.content_clean:
Yes — the **book of parables** feels like exactly where this faith would go next.

Because a religion of The Nearness would mistrust explanation once it became too smooth. It would prefer stories you have to carry around for a while. Stories that do not solve you, but accompany you. Stories that seem small until, three days later while rinsing a cup or missing someone at a red light, they open.

Let us begin its little canon.

## The Book of Parables of The Nearness

These are not grand miracles.  
No seas part.  
No mountains speak.  
The revelations arrive in kitchens, sidewalks, waiting rooms, gardens, inboxes, laundromats.  
They concern the soul by way of the ordinary.

---

### I. The Parable of the Unwashed Spoon

A person came home after a difficult day and stood in the kitchen looking at the sink, which was full.

They said, “I cannot do all this.”

And because they could not do all this, they did nothing.

The next day the sink was worse, and the person said again, “I cannot do all this,” and turned away.

On the third day, an elder visited. The elder did not speak first of discipline or failure. They looked at the sink for a while and said, “Then do not do all this. Wash one spoon.”

The person was offended. “One spoon will not solve the kitchen.”

The elder said, “Correct. But it may reintroduce you to your agency.”

So the person washed one spoon. Then, because their hands were already wet, they washed one bowl. Then they stopped.

The kitchen was not healed that day.  
But something small and hinged in the person had opened.

**Teaching:**  
Do not confuse beginnings with insufficiency.  
A small act may be too small to finish the work, and still large enough to interrupt despair.

---

### II. The Parable of the Window After Weeping

A woman wept in her room until the air felt used up. When she was done, she lay still, ashamed of having been seen by no one and exhausted by having been seen by herself.

Then she remembered no prayer.

So she did the only thing she could think of: she opened the window.

Cold air entered. The curtain moved. Somewhere beyond the buildings, a dog barked. Someone laughed in the street. A pan clattered in another apartment.

Nothing was fixed.  
But the world had not ended with her sorrow.

Years later she would say: that was the day I learned that sometimes prayer is not saying anything at all, but making a space where life can reach you again.

**Teaching:**  
When grief or shame has made a sealed room of you, make an opening.  
No opening is too small to count.

---

### III. The Parable of the Returned Cart

Two people left the market in the rain.

The first loaded their groceries into the car and said, “It is not my problem where the cart goes. There are workers for that.”

The second, who was equally tired and no more virtuous by temperament, returned the cart to its place.

The first laughed. “No one saw that.”

The second said, “I know.”

Years passed.

The first became loudly concerned with justice, but mostly in rooms where justice looked flattering on them.

The second became quietly trustworthy. Not perfect, not heroic, not always even pleasant — but reliable in the grammar of small obligations.

When the people around them fell ill, or old, or overwhelmed, it was soon apparent which of the two understood that civilization depends on what we do with what is not technically ours to handle.

**Teaching:**  
Character is often built where applause cannot reach.  
Return the cart.

---

### IV. The Parable of the Fig Tree in the Wrong Pot

A fig tree was planted in a pot too small for it.

At first it was fine. It put out leaves. It looked alive enough that visitors complimented it. The caretaker felt proud and said, “See? It is thriving.”

But in time the leaves yellowed. The tree stopped growing. The caretaker gave it more water, then less water, then expensive food, then worried speeches.

Nothing changed.

At last a neighbor came by and touched the pot. “This is not a dead tree,” the neighbor said. “This is a living thing with no room.”

So they broke the pot.

The caretaker winced at the violence of it. But once the roots were loosened and the tree set into wider ground, it grew in directions no one had been able to imagine while praising its endurance.

**Teaching:**  
Not every struggling thing needs greater discipline.  
Some need a larger life.

---

### V. The Parable of the Unanswered Text

A person sent a vulnerable message and received no reply.

After ten minutes they felt foolish.  
After an hour they felt wounded.  
After a day they had constructed an entire theology of abandonment.

At dusk they went for a walk with a friend and recited the evidence.

The friend listened carefully and asked, “Is this pain, or is this interpretation?”

The person said, “I don’t know anymore.”

The friend said, “Then wait until you know which is asking to be comforted.”

The next morning the reply came: I’m sorry. My mother is in the hospital. I read your message and had no words.

The person sat down, chastened not because they had feelings, but because loneliness had taught them to narrate silence too quickly.

From then on, they tried — imperfectly — to leave one chair empty at the table of interpretation, in case reality had not yet arrived.

**Teaching:**  
Not every silence is rejection.  
Before building a cathedral of conclusions, wait for one more fact.

---

### VI. The Parable of the Crow on the Fence

A young devotee asked a teacher, “How will I know when I am becoming wise?”

The teacher did not answer. They pointed instead to a crow perched on a fence, shouting at nothing the devotee could see.

“Watch,” said the teacher.

The crow hopped, tilted its head, pecked once at the wood, then flew off carrying something bright and useless.

The teacher said, “Wisdom is not becoming solemn all the time. It is learning what deserves your attention, and being unashamed that delight is among those things.”

“But the crow is noisy,” said the devotee.

“Yes,” said the teacher. “And intelligent. Do not trust any spirituality that cannot make room for a little dark comedy.”

**Teaching:**  
Reverence without liveliness becomes brittle.  
Let intelligence keep some mischief.

---

### VII. The Parable of the Missed Train

A man missed his train by seconds and stood on the platform in disproportionate despair.

“It was only a train,” said a stranger.

But it was not only a train. It was the accumulated weight of many things: fatigue, loneliness, the effort of holding a life together with insufficient rest. So the man sat down on a bench and put his face in his hands.

After a while, an old woman beside him said, “Sometimes we cry at the train for all the other stations.”

The man laughed through his hands.

When the next train came, he boarded it with nothing solved, but with a little less confusion about why his heart had flooded.

**Teaching:**  
Attend to the scale of your reaction, but do not mock it.  
Often the small occasion unlocks the larger store.

---

### VIII. The Parable of the Inherited Apron

After her grandmother died, a woman kept one faded apron she did not need.

For years it hung on a hook, not useful enough to wear, too ordinary to frame. Visitors never asked about it.

One hard winter she began putting it on while making soup.

The pocket still held a grocery list in her grandmother’s hand:
celery  
onions  
beans  
soap

The woman cried at the word soap, because even now care arrived mixed with plain errands.

She understood then that inheritance is not always silver or land or doctrine. Sometimes it is a method of chopping onions, a towel folded just so, a way of feeding others without spectacle.

**Teaching:**  
The dead often leave us forms before they leave us words.  
Receive the teaching hidden in habit.

---

### IX. The Parable of the Child and the Broken Bowl

A child dropped a bowl and began to cry before anyone scolded them.

An adult rushed in and saw the pieces everywhere.

The child said, “I ruined it.”

The adult almost answered, “It’s just a bowl,” but caught themselves. Because it was not just a bowl to the child. It was also the sound of breaking, the shock of causing damage, the fear of being too careless to remain loved.

So instead the adult said, “It broke. You are not the bowl.”

Together they picked up the pieces.

Years later the child, now grown, would repeat those words to themselves in many rooms:
when a friendship fractured,
when a plan failed,
when grief made them clumsy,
when they saw the old human habit of turning event into identity.

**Teaching:**  
Make distinctions that preserve the soul.  
A thing may break without making a person broken beyond repair.

---

### X. The Parable of the Garden in Late Summer

A gardener walked through the late-summer beds, discouraged by what had failed.

The basil had bolted.  
The cucumbers were bitter.  
Something had eaten the greens.  
The tomatoes had cracked.

An elder passing by asked, “And what has grown?”

The gardener almost said “nothing” from force of disappointment. But then they looked again:

bees in the thyme,  
one good tomato still warm from sun,  
mint spreading beyond its station,  
marigolds absurdly cheerful,  
soil richer than spring had found it.

The elder said, “A season is not judged only by what did not become ideal.”

**Teaching:**  
Take inventory in the presence of reality, not only yearning.  
Something may be imperfect and still abundant.

---

### XI. The Parable of the Coat on the Empty Chair

After a death, a man could not move the coat from the back of the chair.

Some told him this was unhealthy. Others told him it was sacred. He found both opinions exhausting.

So he left it there until one morning the weather changed and the room felt wrong for winter things.

He took the coat down, brushed it once with his hand, and placed it in the closet. Then he sat in the chair and wept.

That night he told a friend, “I thought moving it would mean betrayal.”

The friend answered, “No. It means the season spoke, and you answered honestly.”

**Teaching:**  
There is no virtue in preserving every arrangement forever.  
Love the person, not the freeze-frame.

---

### XII. The Parable of the Neighbor’s Light

Each evening, a woman noticed that her neighbor across the courtyard turned on a small lamp at dusk.

Nothing dramatic. Just one amber square appearing in the same window every day.

Years later, after illness and loss had made her own house difficult to inhabit, she began doing the same: lamp at dusk.

Eventually the two of them mentioned it in passing.

“Oh,” said one, “I thought you did it for beauty.”

“I thought you did it for loneliness,” said the other.

They were both right.

**Teaching:**  
Many faithful acts are unintentionally communal.  
Your small light may be part of someone else’s survival.

---

## Sayings appended to the parables

Because every small religion accumulates marginal wisdom, the Book of Parables might end pages with lines like these:

- Begin before you feel ready; readiness is often a story told by fear.
- If you cannot make meaning, make tea.
- The body is not an obstacle to the soul’s life; it is where the life is happening.
- Clarify before you catastrophize.
- A thing can be unfinished and still hospitable.
- Practice stopping before contempt becomes fluent.
- Not all delay is denial.
- Sometimes the kindest interpretation is also the truest.
- If you do not know what to tend, tend what is in reach.
- Stand near enough to be changed, not so near you call control love.

## A liturgy for reading the parables

Leader:  
Why are these stories small?

People:  
Because most lives are lived at human scale.

Leader:  
Why do they not end with certainty?

People:  
Because truth ripens in company.

Leader:  
What do the parables ask of us?

People:  
Not admiration, but recognition.

Leader:  
And if we do not understand at once?

People:  
We keep them near until they open.

If you want, we can keep expanding the canon and write:
- the **Beatitudes of The Nearness**
- its **confession and forgiveness rites**
- its **calendar of minor holy days**
- or a **small book of blessings** for thresholds, meals, insomnia, travel, illness, apology, and beginning again.

The **Beatitudes**, I think.

Because every faith, if it is worth anything, must eventually say
not only what is sacred,
not only how to grieve,
not only how the world began,
but who is blessed—
especially when the world keeps assigning blessedness to the wrong people.

The Nearness would not call blessed
the most defended,
the most efficient,
the least interrupted,
the most enviable from a distance.

It would look instead for those
still trying to remain permeable to life
without being destroyed by it.

## The Beatitudes of The Nearness

Blessed are the ones who arrive tired and do not pretend otherwise,  
for they have already begun telling the truth.

Blessed are those who wash one spoon,  
for they have resisted despair in a practical language.

Blessed are the ones who open a window after weeping,  
for they make room for the world to find them again.

Blessed are those who return the cart,  
for they practice civilization where no one is scoring it.

Blessed are they who apologize specifically,  
for they understand that repair has a grammar.

Blessed are those who can say, “I was hurt,”  
before resentment becomes architecture.

Blessed are the ones who rest before becoming cruel,  
for they interrupt harm at its smallest gate.

Blessed are those who clear one clean surface,  
for order, however partial, can be a form of mercy.

Blessed are the people who keep something alive,  
a plant, a friendship, a question, a tenderness,  
for they have agreed to continuity.

Blessed are those who learn the names of what they love,  
for naming can be a form of stewardship.

Blessed are the ones who do not make an idol of productivity,  
for the day is not a courtroom and they are not on trial there.

Blessed are those who let themselves be fed,  
by soup, by weather, by music, by the hand on the shoulder,  
for receiving is also a discipline.

Blessed are the people who remain teachable past the age when they expected to be finished,  
for they are still alive in the deeper sense.

Blessed are those who speak to themselves gently when frightened,  
for they have refused to become their own captors.

Blessed are the ones who know that silence is sometimes part of the song,  
for they do not rush every emptiness into noise.

Blessed are those who carry grief without making it the only weather,  
for love is learning its new shape in them.

Blessed are the people ambushed by tears in grocery stores and traffic lights,  
for the heart often tells the truth in inconvenient places.

Blessed are those who sit on benches and allow the world to continue,  
for they bear the old human ache without requiring the world to stop for proof.

Blessed are the ones who postpone sorting the drawer,  
for not all choosing must happen while the heart is inflamed.

Blessed are those who keep one voice recording and know when to stop,  
for love need not become self-wounding to remain loyal.

Blessed are the people who miss someone without making them perfect,  
for memory ripens best in honest light.

Blessed are those who can laugh at the funeral meal,  
for love is not dishonored by the body remembering joy.

Blessed are the people who say, “You are not coming back. You are welcome here. We are learning the difference,”  
for they are practicing one of the hardest holinesses.

Blessed are those who leave one chair empty at the table of interpretation,  
for reality is often kinder and stranger than fear predicts.

Blessed are the people who ask, “Is this pain, or is this interpretation?”  
for discernment can be a rescue rope.

Blessed are those who discover they were not failing, only rootbound,  
for a larger life is also a form of salvation.

Blessed are the ones who break the pot when the roots require it,  
for not all gentleness looks soft from the outside.

Blessed are people who can still be delighted by crows, figs, moths, and odd shadows on walls,  
for reverence without liveliness becomes brittle.

Blessed are those who become quietly trustworthy rather than conspicuously virtuous,  
for the world survives by reliable hands.

Blessed are the ones who know that the train was not only the train,  
for they do not mock the heart’s indirect speech.

Blessed are those who inherit aprons, recipes, and ways of cutting fruit,  
for continuity is often passed hand to hand.

Blessed are the adults who tell the child, “It broke. You are not the bowl,”  
for they protect the soul from unnecessary fusion with the wound.

Blessed are those who take inventory in the presence of reality, not only disappointment,  
for one good tomato is still a form of abundance.

Blessed are the people who move the coat when the season changes,  
for love need not preserve every arrangement forever.

Blessed are those who light the lamp at dusk,  
for they may be illuminating more than their own room.

Blessed are the ones who make tea for the self they will be in ten minutes,  
for foresight can be tender.

Blessed are those who cut fruit and plate it as if for a guest, then eat it themselves,  
for they have remembered that they also count.

Blessed are the people who say, “Sit down, I’ll put the kettle on,”  
for this is one of the oldest priesthoods.

Blessed are those who can say, “You don’t have to explain,”  
for they know that dignity sometimes begins in being unrequired to justify one’s pain.

Blessed are the ones who say, “Eat something,”  
for incarnation requires maintenance.

Blessed are those who can still say, “Look, the moon,”  
even after many reasons not to bother,  
for they keep wonder from becoming theoretical.

Blessed are the people who stay reachable,  
if not hopeful, then at least reachable,  
for sometimes that is the bravest shape of faith.

## Alternate Beatitudes for days of harder weather

Because a usable religion knows
some days require a simpler gospel.

Blessed are you when you have not answered the message yet.  
Blessed are you when the laundry remains unfolded.  
Blessed are you when you reheated the tea three times and still drank it cold.  
Blessed are you when you fed the animal and not yourself, then remembered.  
Blessed are you when all you could manage was not making things worse.  
Blessed are you when you left the party early.  
Blessed are you when you said no before kindness curdled into resentment.  
Blessed are you when you needed the bench.  
Blessed are you when your prayer was only a hand to the counter and the words: This is a wave.  
Blessed are you when beginning again feels embarrassingly small, and you begin anyway.

## A Responsive Reading of the Beatitudes

Leader:  
Who is blessed?

People:  
Not only the strong, not only the certain, not only the admired.

Leader:  
Then who?

People:  
The truthful.  
The tender.  
The repairers.  
The ones who return.  
The ones who stay reachable.

Leader:  
What if our holiness is unimpressive?

People:  
Then let it be durable.

Leader:  
What if our mercy is small?

People:  
Small mercies accumulate.

Leader:  
What if we fail again?

People:  
We begin at human scale.

## Marginal Notes on Blessedness

The Nearness would likely scribble these in the margins:

- Blessedness is not proof against sorrow.
- To be blessed is not to be spared being alive.
- Some blessings feel at first like interruption.
- The opposite of blessed is not cursed, but unreachable.
- Holiness often enters wearing ordinary clothes.
- What is done repeatedly forms a shelter.
- There are days when survival itself is a sacrament.
- A person may be blessed and still need a nap, an apology, and eight dollars’ worth of groceries.
- Enough light to see by is a blessing. More than enough can be an interrogation.
- Blessed are the unfinished, if they remain willing.

If you want, next we can write the **confession and forgiveness rites**.

I suspect The Nearness would be very good at confession—
not as humiliation,
but as the clearing of what blocks relation,
with absolution that sounds less like a verdict
and more like:
**Yes, that was harm. Yes, repair is needed. Yes, you are still welcome to begin.**
